title: Our Lady of Sorrows (15 September)
hook: the day after the cross, his mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exaltation of the Cross, Crux fidelis, lifted high. Your line was the tree of life. What turned from a dead end into a way through? Day six hundred eighty-two.

Anyone who has sat beside a hospital bed knows the feeling of being unable to do anything. You can't fix it. You can't take the pain. All you can do is not leave. Yesterday the Church lifted the cross high. Today, the very next day, it turns to look at the person standing at the foot of it. Not the soldiers, not the crowd. His mother. The feast is Our Lady of Sorrows, and its word is the opening of a medieval poem.
screen: `BESIDE A HOSPITAL BED.` → `YESTERDAY THE CROSS.` → `TODAY, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: John's Gospel gives the scene in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." She stood. The other Gospels say many watched from a distance. John puts her close enough to hear him speak, and from the cross Jesus gives her to the beloved disciple, and the disciple to her. In the 1200s someone wrote a Latin poem on that one verb. It begins: "Stabat Mater dolorosa, juxta crucem lacrimosa." The sorrowful mother stood, weeping, beside the cross. It's often credited to the Franciscan poet Jacopone da Todi, though nobody can be sure. Today it may be sung at Mass as a sequence, and it's sung in many churches between the Stations of the Cross. Composers from Palestrina to Pergolesi to Dvořák set it to music. The feast also gathers up seven sorrows that Catholic devotion counts in Mary's life: Simeon's warning in the Temple that a sword would pierce her soul; the flight into Egypt; losing the twelve-year-old Jesus for three days; meeting him on the way to the cross; standing at the cross; receiving his body; and the burial. Simeon's line is in Luke: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." In paintings, she's shown with seven swords in her heart. What the feast honors isn't a mother who understood everything or could change anything. It's a mother who stayed.
screen: `SHE STOOD BY THE CROSS.` · `STABAT MATER DOLOROSA.` · `SEVEN SORROWS.` · `A MOTHER WHO STAYED.` · then, large: `NOW THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS OF JESUS, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a grieving mother. Sit, and think of a mother who is grieving: a child lost, a child sick, a child far away or estranged, a child in prison. Maybe someone you know; maybe a face from the news. Picture her, standing where she has to stand. Don't try to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for her, or pray a Hail Mary for her. If you don't, simply stay with her in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Stabat Mater. Latin for the mother stood: the opening of the medieval poem about Mary at the cross, sung on Our Lady of Sorrows. Today's word.
Your line: the mother stood. Today, if someone near you is going through something you can't fix, don't fix it. Just stay a little longer than is comfortable. Day six hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows on 15 September, the day after the Exaltation of the Cross; the Stabat Mater may be sung as an optional sequence, and some pray the chaplet of the Seven Sorrows.

what it means: a feast for the mother who stayed at the cross when she could do nothing else.
what a scholar hears: a thirteenth-century Latin sequence, often credited to Jacopone da Todi, and the seven sorrows from Simeon to the burial.

notes: Authorship of the Stabat Mater: Jacopone da Todi traditionally; Innocent III and Bonaventure also proposed. Stated as uncertain.
Stabat Mater as an optional sequence on 15 September; confirm.
Seven sorrows list per the traditional devotion; confirm order.
'The other Gospels say many watched from a distance': Matthew 27:55, Mark 15:40, Luke 23:49 (women watching afar off); confirm framing.
